title: No. 74 — The Command of the Military and Naval Forces, and the Pardoning Power of the Executive. (Hamilton)
paragraphs: The President of the United States is to be "commander-in-chief of the army and navy of the United States, and of the militia of the several States when called into the actual service of the United States." The propriety of this provision is so evident in itself, and so much in line with the precedents of the state constitutions in general, that little need be said to explain or defend it. Even those state constitutions that, in other respects, pair the chief magistrate with a council have for the most part concentrated military authority in him alone. Of all the concerns of government, the direction of war most particularly demands the qualities that distinguish the exercise of power by a single hand. The direction of war implies the direction of the common strength, and the power of directing and employing the common strength forms a usual and essential part of the definition of executive authority.

"The President may require the opinion, in writing, of the principal officer in each of the executive departments, upon any subject relating to the duties of their respective offices." I consider this a mere redundancy in the plan, since the right it provides for would follow naturally from the office itself.

He is also authorized to grant "reprieves and pardons for offenses against the United States, except in cases of impeachment." Humanity and good policy together dictate that the benign prerogative of pardon should be as little fettered or embarrassed as possible. The criminal code of every country has so much necessary severity that without easy access to exceptions in favor of unfortunate guilt, justice would wear a countenance too bloody and cruel. Since the sense of responsibility is always strongest in proportion as it is undivided, it may be inferred that a single man would be most ready to attend to the force of those motives that might plead for mitigating the rigor of the law, and least apt to yield to considerations calculated to shelter a fit object of its vengeance. The thought that the fate of a fellow human being depended on his sole decision would naturally inspire scrupulousness and caution. The dread of being accused of weakness or connivance would breed equal circumspection, though of a different kind. On the other hand, since men generally draw confidence from their numbers, they might often encourage each other in an act of obstinacy, and might be less sensitive to the threat of suspicion or censure for injudicious or affected clemency. For these reasons, one man appears to be a more suitable dispenser of the mercy of government than a body of men.

The expediency of vesting the power of pardon in the President has, if I am not mistaken, been contested only in relation to the crime of treason. It has been urged that this should have depended on the assent of one or both branches of the legislative body. I shall not deny that strong reasons can be given for requiring on this point the concurrence of that body, or part of it. Since treason is a crime aimed at the very being of society, once the laws have ascertained the guilt of the offender, there seems a fitness in referring the expediency of an act of mercy toward him to the judgment of the legislature. And this should be the case all the more because the supposition of the Chief Magistrate's connivance ought not to be entirely excluded. But there are also strong objections to such a plan. It cannot be doubted that a single man of prudence and good sense is better fitted, in delicate situations, to weigh the motives that may plead for and against the remission of punishment than any numerous body whatever. It deserves particular attention that treason will often be connected with seditions involving a large proportion of the community — as recently happened in Massachusetts. In every such case, we might expect to see the representation of the people tainted with the same spirit that gave birth to the offense. And when parties were fairly evenly matched, the secret sympathy of the condemned person's friends and supporters, taking advantage of the good nature and weakness of others, might frequently grant impunity where the terror of an example was necessary. On the other hand, when the sedition had arisen from causes that had inflamed the resentments of the majority party, they might often be obstinate and inexorable, when policy required forbearance and clemency. But the chief argument for placing the pardon power, in this case, in the Chief Magistrate is this: in seasons of insurrection or rebellion, there are often critical moments when a well-timed offer of pardon to the insurgents or rebels may restore the tranquility of the commonwealth — moments which, if allowed to pass unused, may never be recalled afterwards. The slow process of convening the legislature, or one of its branches, to obtain its sanction for the measure would frequently mean letting the golden opportunity slip. The loss of a week, a day, an hour, may sometimes be fatal. If it is suggested that a discretionary power, with such contingencies in view, might occasionally be conferred on the President, the answer is, first, that it is questionable whether, in a limited Constitution, such power could be delegated by law; and second, that it would generally be impolitic to take any step beforehand that might hold out the prospect of impunity. Such a proceeding, outside the usual course, would likely be construed as an argument of timidity or weakness and would tend to embolden guilt.
